title: Monitoring and alerts
summary: How to find out your app is broken before your users tell you: error tracking, uptime checks, logs, analytics, and alerts that wake you only when it matters.
youWillLearn: The four signals of a live app and the question each one answers
How error tracking like Sentry turns a crash into a readable report
What to log for an AI feature, and what never to log
How to set alerts that are rare, clear and worth waking up for

glossary.monitoring: Watching a live app with tools, so problems show up on a dashboard or as an alert instead of in an angry email.
glossary.error tracking: A service that catches crashes in your app, groups identical ones, and shows where in the code they happened.
glossary.stack trace: The list of function calls that led to an error, file by file and line by line. It points at where things broke.
glossary.uptime check: An outside service that visits a web address of your app every minute or so and alerts you if it does not answer correctly.
glossary.health check: A small address in your app, like /api/health, that answers whether the app and its key parts are working.
glossary.log: A line of text your app writes when something happens, with a timestamp, kept so you can read it later.
glossary.structured logging: Writing logs as JSON (named fields and values) so you can filter and count them instead of reading walls of text.
glossary.product analytics: Counting what users do (sign-ups, clicks, features used) to see whether the app is used as intended.
glossary.alert fatigue: When alerts fire so often that people stop reacting to them, including the one that matters.
glossary.PII: Personally identifiable information: anything that points to a real person, like an email, a name or a note's content.

steps.title: Notely is live, and you are busy
body: Five thousand people use Notely. Their clicks reach the app server, the computer running Notely's code, which asks the Claude API (Anthropic's AI) for each summary.
You build Notely, and you spend your days on new features. Nothing watches the live app for you. If it breaks, you hear about it when someone tells you.

scene.caption: Users reach the app server, which calls the Claude API. You are busy elsewhere.

steps.title: Your users find out first
body: On Tuesday, the Summarize button starts failing for every user. The page shows a spinner forever.
You find out three hours later, from an email titled "is this broken??". You have no idea when it started, how many people were hit, or what the error even says.

callout.text: A shop with no smoke detector. You learn about the fire when a neighbor knocks on your door.

changes: ~ App Server → Claude API: every summary fails
+ An email from users reaches you, hours late
~ Time to notice Unknown → 3 hours

scene.caption: Summaries fail for hours. You learn it from an email.

steps.title: Four signals, four questions
body: Monitoring gives a live app eyes. Four signals cover most of it.

Errors: what broke, and where in the code? Uptime: can anyone reach the app at all? Logs: what exactly happened on that request? Analytics: are people using it the way you expect? Each answers a question the others cannot.
changes: − 5,000 users, Claude API and You: we focus on the app server
+ Errors, Uptime, Logs, Analytics: four ways to watch it

scene.caption: Four signals around the app server, one on each side.

steps.title: Error tracking: crashes become reports
body: An error tracking service like Sentry catches crashes in the browser and on the server. It groups repeats and shows the stack trace (the code path to the crash), the deploy it came from and how many users were hit.
Errors your code handles itself, like a Claude timeout, you send on purpose, with tags to filter by.

code.caption: The user gets a clear message instead of a spinner. You get the full error.

changes: ~ Errors: every failed summary arrives as a report
~ Uptime, Logs, Analytics step back

scene.caption: Each crash in the app server becomes one grouped report.

steps.title: Uptime checks: someone knocking
body: Error tracking runs inside your app. If the app is down completely, it cannot report anything.

An uptime check is an outside service that visits your app every minute. Point it at a health check like /api/health: a small address that also tests the database, so "up" means truly working, not only "the server answered".

code.caption: GET answers a visit. Status 503 tells the checker "not working right now". No Claude call here, or each knock would cost money.

changes: ~ Uptime: knocks on the app every minute, from outside
~ Errors steps back

scene.caption: An outside service knocks on the health check every minute.

steps.title: Logs: the diary of every request
body: A log is a line your code writes when something happens. Use structured logging: named fields, so you can filter by user or count slow calls.
For an AI feature, log the model, the tokens used (the units AI is billed in), the time taken and the outcome. That reveals a slow model or a cost spike.

code.caption: Hosting logs are often kept only for a short time. Send them to a log service if you need history.

changes: ~ Logs: one structured line per summary
~ Uptime steps back

scene.caption: Every summary writes one line to the logs.

steps.title: Analytics: the quiet failures
body: Some breakage throws no error. A button hidden by a styling change. A summary that comes back empty. The app is "up", and nobody uses the feature.
Product analytics counts what users do. If summaries per hour drop from 300 to zero after a deploy, that is a bug report, even with a clean error log.

callout.text: As a designer you already read funnels. Track the steps of the core flow (open note, click Summarize, see summary) and the drop-off between them is your early warning.

changes: ~ Analytics: summaries per hour fall to zero
~ Logs steps back

scene.caption: No errors, but the summary count drops to zero.

steps.title: Alerts that are worth waking for
body: Signals are useless if nobody looks. Alerts push the important ones to your phone.

Alert on what users feel: the site is down, a new error hits many users, errors jump after a deploy. Everything else goes into a daily summary email. Too many pings cause alert fatigue, and the real one gets ignored.

callout.text: When Claude Code sets up Sentry, check: is its key (the DSN) in an environment variable, not in the code? Do alert rules fire only for production? Are source maps uploaded, so traces show real file names? Is sendDefaultPii (send users' personal data) off?

changes: + You: get an alert on your phone
~ Errors and Uptime alert you; Logs and Analytics go in a daily email
~ Time to notice 3 hours → 2 min
~ Alerts a day 0 → 3

scene.caption: Only errors and downtime reach your phone.

steps.title: Logs are a copy of your data
body: The tempting debug line logs the whole request or the whole prompt. Now every user's note, email and login token sits in an outside log service, kept for weeks, readable by anyone on the account.
Log ids and numbers, not content. Never log PII (anything that points to a person), note text, API keys or login headers.

callout.text: A client's privacy policy usually promises where their data goes. A log line with note content quietly breaks that promise, and logs are rarely covered by your delete-my-account flow.

code.code:
- console.log('summary request', req.headers, note.body);
+ console.log(JSON.stringify({ event: 'ai_summary', noteId }));
code.caption: Same debugging value, none of the private data.

changes: ~ Logs: now hold private note text and login tokens
~ Errors, Uptime and You step back

scene.caption: One careless log line copies private notes into another company's tool.

steps.title: Recap: eyes on the live app
body: Errors show what broke and where. Uptime checks catch a dead app. Logs show what happened on one request. Analytics catch quiet failures that throw no error.
Alert only on what users feel, and log ids and numbers, never private content.
changes: ~ Logs: ids and numbers only
~ All four signals and your alerts back in view

scene.caption: Four signals, two alerts, and logs without private data.

quiz.question: Notely's server is completely down. Which signal tells you first?

options.text: Sentry, because it catches every error.
options.why: Sentry runs inside the app. If the app is not running, there is nothing to send the error.

options.text: An uptime check calling /api/health from outside.
options.why: It runs on someone else's servers, so it notices when your app stops answering, and it alerts within minutes.
Events would stop, but analytics tools are not built to alert in minutes on a full outage.

quiz.question: Claude Code added this line to debug the summary route: console.log(req.headers, note.body). What do you ask it to do?

options.text: Keep it. Logs are private to your team.
options.why: Logs live in an outside tool, are kept for a while and are seen by everyone with access. The headers include login tokens.

options.text: Move it to the browser console instead.
options.why: The browser cannot see server-side failures, and the headers would still be exposed.

options.text: Log a structured event with ids, model, tokens and timing instead.
options.why: That keeps the debugging value without copying private notes and login headers into your log provider.

quiz.question: You get about 40 alerts a day, mostly warnings from preview builds. Last night you slept through a real outage. What should change?

options.text: Alert only on user-facing problems in production, and send the rest to a digest.
options.why: Alert fatigue made the real alert invisible. Fewer, clearer alerts get acted on. Tagging the environment keeps preview noise out.

options.text: Turn alerts up to the loudest sound.
options.why: Louder noise does not help when most of it is meaningless. People mute or ignore it.

options.text: Turn off alerts and check the dashboard every morning.
options.why: Then an outage at 11 p.m. runs all night. Alerts are needed; they need to be rare and meaningful.

takeaways: Watch four signals: errors, uptime, logs and analytics. Each answers a different question.
Use an error tracker like Sentry, and send handled errors to it with tags like feature: 'ai-summary'.
Point an outside uptime check at a /api/health route that also tests the database.
Log structured events with ids, model, tokens and timing. Never log private content, tokens or keys.
Alert only on what users feel. Too many alerts and the important one gets ignored.
